papers.introduction: The study aimed to measure and compare adolescent girls' knowledge and skills about digital tools, their importance and practical use, across three phases of a Digital Literacy Training Program (DLTP).
papers.methodology: A quasi-experimental design compared an intervention arm with a comparison arm at baseline (2017), midline (2019) and endline (2020). Participants were adolescent girls aged 14–19 years in six intervention and two comparison blocks of District Gumla, Jharkhand, selected by multistage sampling. Sample sizes were 314 vs 272 at baseline, 318 vs 260 at midline and 402 vs 202 at endline. Data came from a semi-structured questionnaire.
papers.theory: Digital literacy was scored by combining questions according to the elements of a digital literacy framework (five elements), cited from prior work.
papers.results: Above-median digital literacy scores were similar at baseline (22.9% vs 17.3%, p=0.1). At midline the intervention arm was higher, 63.8% vs 41.2% (p=0.00), and at endline 90% vs 41.6% (p=0.00). Endline total DL median was 27 (20–33) in the intervention arm and 12 (9–17) in the comparison arm. Knowledge and uptake of government schemes above 6 was 60.2% vs 32.7% at endline (p=0.00).
papers.discussion: The authors conclude the programme led to improved digital literacy scores in the intervention arms compared with comparison blocks, and that this in turn led to raising awareness and uptake of government schemes. They cannot fully attribute the change to the programme, as household possessions rose and might have contributed. Limitations include loss to follow-up. They call for scale-up of such programmes to bridge the existing digital divide.

papers.introduction: The study evaluated a 6-week digital literacy and digital wellbeing program. It tested whether the program showed more favorable pre-to-post changes in PIU, DSE and DGI than a wait-list control group. A second aim was to examine whether post-intervention data were statistically consistent with a serial pathway linking condition, DSE, DGI and PIU.
papers.methodology: Two-arm, parallel-group quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design in Hubei Province, China, conducted in March and April 2026. Of 206 adolescents, 103 were allocated by quota to the intervention and 103 to wait-list control. Eligible adolescents were aged 12–18. Outcomes were self-reported, measured with the SPIUT, the AIAS Internet Self-Efficacy subscale and the short-form DGI. Analysis used 2 × 2 repeated-measures ANOVA and PROCESS Model 6.
papers.theory: The I-PACE model was used to guide the intervention logic. Social Cognitive Theory is cited as a rationale for considering DSE before self-regulation, which the concurrent data cannot determine.
papers.results: Group × Time interactions were significant for PIU, F(1, 204) = 13.75, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.063; DGI, F(1, 204) = 26.53, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.115; and DSE, F(1, 204) = 18.62, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.084. The wait-list change in DGI was not statistically significant, t(102) = −1.36, p = 0.176. The serial path from intervention via DSE and DGI to PIU was significant, B = −2.589; the two single-mediator paths showed no significance.
papers.discussion: The authors suggest a structured digital literacy program may be a useful educational approach for supporting healthier Internet use among adolescents. They state the mediation findings are statistical consistency with a theory-informed pathway, not definitive evidence of temporal order or causal reduction of PIU. Limitations include non-random assignment, self-reported outcomes, absence of assessor blinding, and digital literacy not being measured.

papers.introduction: The study aims to describe lower secondary technology teachers’ experiences of teaching digital models using digital tools. Its research question asks how these teachers experience this teaching. Very little is known about it in compulsory schools today.
papers.methodology: Twelve semi-structured interviews were held with lower secondary technology teachers (five males, seven females) at their schools, from October 2018 to September 2019. Teachers had 1 to 19 years in service. Interviews lasted 35 to 60 minutes and used an open interview guide. Thematic analysis followed.
papers.theory: The study is framed by a phenomenological lifeworld approach as its ontological and epistemological approach. Experience is understood as respondents’ knowledge, beliefs, purposes and intentions related to teaching digital models.
papers.results: The study describes four themes of teachers’ experiences: enhancing and integrating other subjects, visualizing technology to the pupils, enabling digital modelling, and preparing pupils for the future. The themes partly overlap. Teachers did not experience digital models as one single idea but as an amalgam of multiple ideas.
papers.discussion: The authors state there is not one way to experience or teach digital models. They say teachers did not share a common knowledge base during the interviews. They conclude discussions need to be more nuanced and specific to provide a common knowledge base. A topic for further research can be how digital models affect pupils’ learning or interest in technology.

papers.introduction: The study aims to examine whether prospective teachers’ use of DVRs affects their TPACK. Prospective teachers face a gap between theory and classroom practice. Two research questions ask about the impact of DVR use on TPACK and its seven domains.
papers.methodology: Quasi-experimental pre- and post-survey design with experimental and control groups, plus interviews. 70 prospective teachers (35 per group) from four specializations, at Al-Qasmi Academic College of Education, Baqa, Israel, in the second semester of 2022/2023. Instruments: a 53-item TPACK questionnaire and interviews with 10 experimental-group participants. Analysis: Quade’s test, paired t-tests, thematic analysis.
papers.theory: The TPACK framework is this study's conceptual framework and analytical tool. It is based on Shulman's PCK framework.
papers.results: Quade’s test found the group difference significant in all seven domains and the overall scale (p 0.001 in each; TCK F 36.356, n2 0.348). Adjusted post-survey TCK means were 47.37 (experimental) and 23.63 (control). The experimental group improved significantly in perceptions of TPACK domains (TCK t 5.480, p 0.001); the control group did not (TCK t 0.382, p 0.352).
papers.discussion: The authors report a significant and positive impact on TPACK for the experimental group and state that the results indicate that the use of DVRs by prospective and in-service teachers is recommended, especially when teachers discuss DVRs in a group. Limitations named: the inability to provide unified control and experimental groups, and self-reported responses.
